title: The Faithful Ledger
premise: In 1911, Freya Thackeray drives for suffragist leader Edith Marchmont, secretly reading the letters she carries and keeping her own coded ledger of what people entrust to her. When a census taker's probing questions expose that Edith has been falsifying membership records to protect informants inside Parliament, Freya realizes the official record will bury the truth of who really won them their vote. Racing against the government historians already writing their version, Freya must choose between loyalty to the woman who gave her a place in the world and getting an honest account on the record. In the end, she testifies under her own name, loses Edith's trust, but deposits her ledger with the national archive — ensuring the truth outlives both of them.
about_author: Y. M. Winterbourne is the pen name of a former archivist who spent a decade cataloguing suffrage-era correspondence in regional collections. They write historical fiction about the people history recorded only in margins.

chapters.title: What Can Be Carried
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. We meet her through her ritual: reading letters by lamplight before delivery, recording confidences in a shorthand ledger, measuring her life in portable things since her family's eviction. She delivers a letter revealing someone inside Parliament is feeding Edith information. Emotional beat: quiet belonging — Freya believes she has finally found a home worth serving.

chapters.title: The Question Too Many
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. The census taker, Mr. Aldous, notices discrepancies between Edith's household returns and the membership rolls Freya carries. His gentle interrogation forces Freya to lie for the first time — and to realize Edith has been erasing names from the record, including a dead informant's. Emotional beat: the first crack; loyalty curdles into suspicion as Freya understands the ledger she keeps may be the only honest one.

chapters.title: The Victor's Draft
chapters.summary: Alternating POV between Freya and Edith. A government historian visits, gathering material for an official commemorative volume, and Edith performs a sanitized version of events while ordering Freya to burn compromising letters. Freya secretly copies them instead. Confronted, Edith admits the falsifications were protection — but Freya sees ambition too. Emotional beat: betrayal and resolve; Freya chooses truth over belonging.

chapters.title: On the Record
chapters.summary: Freya's POV. She gives sworn testimony to the historian, naming the erased informant and producing her ledger, knowing it ends her employment and her found family. Edith denounces her publicly, yet privately leaves Freya the motorcar — acknowledgment without forgiveness. Freya deposits the ledger with the national archive under her own name. Emotional beat: costly peace; memory secured, belonging rebuilt on honest ground.
